analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal construction contractors to pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage law, backed by 65 House Republicans, was never considered by any committee or by the full House and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, in place since 1931, requires companies working on federally financed construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage for their trade. This bill would wipe that requirement out entirely. Supporters argued it would lower construction costs for the government; critics say it would cut the pay of construction workers on public projects and shift money from workers' wages to contractors' bottom lines.
analysis.who_benefits: Government contractors, who would save on labor costs by paying market rates instead of prevailing wages on federal construction jobs — savings that could also lower government construction bids.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the requirement that contractors on federally financed building projects pay the locally prevailing wage to laborers and mechanics.
Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act in its entirety with a single section, ending its wage and overtime protections for workers on federal public works contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally financed projects, who would lose the guarantee of locally prevailing wages, potentially taking significant pay cuts on public works jobs.

drawbacks.text: Repealing prevailing-wage requirements would remove the wage floor for laborers and mechanics on federal construction, letting contractors pay lower market rates on public projects.
The Davis-Bacon Act is the only federal statute guaranteeing prevailing wages on federal construction, so its repeal would leave workers on those jobs with no prevailing-wage protection at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — lower labor costs for government construction — would go to contractors and possibly taxpayers, while its cost would fall directly on construction workers' wages on public projects. The transfer runs from workers to contractors, and the bill offered no offsetting protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, passed along to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tom DeLay introduced the bill on June 10, 1993 to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act.
Sixty-four Republicans joined DeLay as cosponsors; all cosponsors were Republicans.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on June 10, 1993.
On June 29, 1993 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety, where it stayed.
No further action was taken in the 103rd Congress, which ended January 3, 1995; the bill never reached a committee or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally financed projects are better off, because the prevailing-wage guarantee they relied on was never repealed. Contractors hoping to cut labor costs on federal jobs did not get that opportunity.

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; it was sent to a subcommittee and received no hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat in committee during a Congress in which Democrats held the House majority.

industries.note: Repeal would have let contractors pay lower market wages instead of prevailing wages on federally financed jobs, cutting labor costs at the expense of workers' pay.
The people whose wages Davis-Bacon guarantees would have lost the wage floor on federal construction projects.
